AK.assessmentBasis: AS 29.45.110(a): the assessor assesses property at full and true value as of 1 January, which the statute defines as "the estimated price that the property would bring in an open market and under the then prevailing market conditions in a sale between a willing seller and a willing buyer both conversant with the property and with prevailing general price levels". No ratio or classification is applied.
AK.derivedArvCaveat: The definition is a market price and the ratio is 1.0, so the derivation is sound in principle. The practical limit is thinness: most of Alaska is served by small assessment offices and much of it has few arm's-length sales to calibrate against, so an assessment in a remote borough is a considered estimate rather than a measurement. Access is the other unmodelled factor — a parcel off the road system is worth a fraction of an equivalent one on it, and nothing in an assessed value or a max bid captures that.
AK.statute: AS §§ 29.45.400 (redemption period, one-year hold), 29.45.440 (expiration), 29.45.450 (deed to borough or city), 29.45.460 (disposition and sale; ordinances required), 29.45.470 (repurchase by record owner within 10 years), 29.45.480 (proceeds of tax sale); AS 29.45.110 (full and true value)
caveats: THE FORMER OWNER HAS TEN YEARS TO TAKE IT BACK, UP UNTIL THE SALE. AS 29.45.470(a) lets the record owner at foreclosure or their assigns repurchase "within 10 years and before the sale or contract of sale", paying the judgment amount plus interest not exceeding 15% a year, accrued taxes, and the municipality's costs of foreclosure, maintenance, insurance and management. A completed sale ends the right, so a buyer's title is safe — but an Alaska listing is reclaimable until the moment it is sold, and due diligence spent on one can evaporate.

TWO ORDINANCES STAND BETWEEN A FORECLOSED PARCEL AND A SALE. Under AS 29.45.460 the municipality must first determine by ordinance whether to retain the property for a public purpose, and if it is held for one, must determine by a further ordinance that no public need exists before it may be sold, with certified mail notice to the former record owner. Adoption of a retention ordinance also extinguishes the repurchase right. Alaska inventory moves at the pace of an assembly agenda.

MOST OF ALASKA HAS NO PROPERTY TAX AT ALL. Only organised boroughs and cities levy one, so the unorganised borough — the majority of the state's area — generates no tax foreclosures and will never appear in this pipeline. Alaska inventory is a handful of municipalities, not a state-wide market.
quietTitle costs here are a placeholder and have not been reviewed by the operator.

AR.assessmentBasis: Arkansas assesses real property at 20% of true, actual or market value (A.C.A. § 26-26-303(c)); § 26-26-304 fails a county whose ratio study falls outside 18–22% of full fair market value. Measured across 1,669 Arkansas parcels carrying both figures, assessed/market was exactly 0.2000 on every one.
AR.statute: A.C.A. § 26-37-202(e) (redemption ends 4:00 p.m. CST the last business day before sale); § 26-37-203 (limited warranty deed; 90-day contest bar); Act 241 of 2023 (removed post-sale redemption); § 26-26-303(c) (20% assessment ratio); § 18-12-609 (challenge period)
caveats: COSL conveys by limited warranty deed and warrants nothing about title. A quiet title or confirmation action is needed for marketability, and title insurance being unavailable is expressly not grounds to cancel the sale.

The 90-day window to contest the conveyance (§ 26-37-203) is a title risk, not a redemption right, and extends to two years after removal of disability for minors, the incapacitated, and wartime service members.

HISTORICAL OUTCOMES BEFORE MID-2023 ARE A DIFFERENT REGIME. Act 241 of 2023 removed post-sale redemption; Arkansas results recorded under the prior rules describe a redeemable position and must not be pooled with post-Act sales when fitting a redemption rate. Current inventory is entirely post-Act.
Quiet-title cost is market practice, not statute — no Arkansas bar fee survey publishes one. The range is an operator estimate; a contested action or curative work costs materially more.

SURVIVING LIENS ARE NOT PRICED HERE. Municipal code-enforcement and clean-up liens (§ 14-54-903) and special improvement district assessments can survive and are parcel-specific — 'HARDING DRAIN IMP DISTRICT' appears on Jefferson County parcels in our own data. IRS liens turn on notice and keep a 120-day redemption right if notice was defective. Mortgages, state tax liens and judgment liens are generally extinguished where COSL gave proper statutory notice. Check each parcel; the closing contingency does not cover these.
The published opening bid is taxes, penalties, interest and costs — the statutory minimum bid under § 26-37-202, never an assessed or market value.

The 90-day contest bar is not absolute. § 26-37-203(d) preserves a taxpayer's right to contest the deed on the ground that the taxes were actually paid, with no 90-day limit stated — a residual challenge route that outlives the window and is the reason to check payment history rather than only the notice trail. § 26-37-203(b)(2) tolls the bar for two years after removal of disability for minors, the mentally incapacitated, and those serving in the armed forces in time of war.

§ 26-37-203(c) cuts the other way and favours the purchaser: a deed issued after 1 January 1987 is not void or voidable merely because the county failed to strictly comply with the tax-delinquent land laws.

redemption.extendedFor: interest is bid down at auction from a 16% statutory maximum

AZ.assessmentBasis: Arizona uses Limited Property Value, which lags full cash value and is capped at 5% annual growth (A.R.S. § 42-13301).
AZ.statute: A.R.S. Title 42, ch. 18 (tax liens and foreclosure)
caveats: Arizona sells liens, not deeds — the usual outcome is redemption with interest, not property ownership.
Taking title requires a separate judicial foreclosure after 3 years, at additional legal cost.
16% is the maximum; competitive auctions routinely bid the rate into low single digits.

CA.assessmentBasis: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 401: property is assessed at full cash value, so the statutory ratio is 1.0.
CA.derivedArvCaveat: California assesses at full cash value, but Proposition 13 fixes the base year and factors it forward at up to 2%/yr. On a long-held parcel the assessed value can sit far below market, so an ARV derived from it understates the property — get comparable sales before bidding.
CA.statute: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code §§ 3691–3731 (tax-defaulted property sales)
caveats: No post-sale redemption. The owner's right ends at 5pm on the last business day before the sale, so the deed conveys without that overhang.
Proposition 13 means assessed value systematically understates market value on long-held parcels. Do not treat a ratio-derived ARV as an appraisal in California.
RTC § 3711 makes the tax deed presumptively valid, so quiet title is optional rather than required — but most title insurers still want it before writing a policy.
Some non-residential commercial property reaches power-to-sell after 3 years of default rather than the usual 5 (RTC § 3691).
Recorded San Diego sale lists mark pre-sale cures as 'REDEEMED'. That is the owner paying before the auction, not a post-sale redemption, and it is quarantined in the copilot's label rules.

CO.assessmentBasis: Colorado assesses residential property at two rates since SB24-233. For school district purposes the 2026 residential rate is 7.05% of actual value; for local government purposes 6.95% is applied to actual value less the lesser of 10% of actual value or $70,000 as adjusted for inflation, an effective rate near 6.26% below $700,000. Commercial and agricultural property is 25% for 2026, down from 27% in 2025. This entry uses the school rate, the higher of the two residential figures.
CO.derivedArvCaveat: Colorado's residential and nonresidential rates differ by a factor of three and a half — about 7% against 25% — so deriving an ARV for a commercial, industrial or agricultural parcel at the residential ratio overstates it roughly 3.5x, which is the dangerous direction and the largest such gap in this file. Confirm the classification before accepting a derived Colorado value. The rates themselves also change almost every year: 27% became 25% between 2025 and 2026, and the residential rates have moved every session since the Gallagher Amendment was repealed in 2020. An out-of-date asOf here means the ratio is simply wrong, not that a statute might have been amended.
CO.statute: C.R.S. §§ 39-11-101 et seq. (tax lien sales), 39-12-103 (redemption and interest), 39-11-120 et seq. (treasurer's deeds) as amended by HB24-1056 (public auction of the option for a treasurer's deed, effective 2024-07-01); SB24-233 (assessment rates)
caveats: THE LIEN NO LONGER BECOMES THE PROPERTY. Since 1 July 2024 (HB24-1056) the county auctions an option for a treasurer's deed to the highest bidder rather than deeding the parcel to the certificate holder, who takes it only if no one bids above the minimum. Colorado is now an interest-only instrument in the ordinary case. Do not model a Colorado lien on the deed remainder, and discount every pre-2024 Colorado guide accordingly.

THE PREMIUM IS A DEAD LOSS, NOT AN INVESTMENT. Colorado bidders compete by bidding a premium above the taxes owed, and per the El Paso County treasurer that overbid "is credited to the county general fund and is not recovered by the investor". It is never returned and it earns no interest — interest accrues only on the tax amount. The real yield is therefore 13% x taxes / (taxes + premium), and a bidder who pays a 30% premium has turned a 13% instrument into a 10% one while also losing the premium outright. The tier below is the statutory rate on the taxes, not the yield on the money spent.

THE RATE IS RESET EVERY YEAR AND THIS ENTRY IS ONE YEAR'S NUMBER. C.R.S. 39-12-103(3) fixes it at nine points over the federal discount rate on 1 September, so the 13% here belongs to liens sold in 2026. A lien keeps its own sale year's rate, which means a portfolio bought across several years earns several different rates.
An unredeemed certificate expires on the fifteenth anniversary of the sale. A holder who neither redeems nor pursues the deed option loses the lien entirely.
quietTitle costs here are a placeholder and have not been reviewed by the operator, and they price a deed process that has existed only since July 2024.

FL.assessmentBasis: Florida assesses at just value, but Save Our Homes / Amendment 1 caps compress assessed below market on long-held homesteads.
caveats: Governmental liens (municipal code enforcement, some special assessments) can survive a Florida tax deed — check the specific municipality.
Federal tax liens survive with a 120-day IRS right of redemption after the sale.
Most title insurers will not insure until a quiet title action completes, and many not until a year after recording.

redemption.extendedFor: redemption stays open indefinitely until the purchaser forecloses it by statutory notice (barment)

GA.assessmentBasis: Georgia assesses at 40% of fair market value (O.C.G.A. § 48-5-7).
caveats: The 12-month period is a minimum, not an expiry — the redemption right persists until you serve barment notice, so budget for that process.
A redeemable deed conveys no right of possession during the redemption period.

redemption.extendedFor: owner-occupied principal residence of 1–6 dwelling units (30 months); most other property redeems at 24 months

bidDown.note: 81.4% of recorded Cook County liens cleared at a 0% penalty bid. Institutional buyers take these for the deed remainder rather than the interest, so expected return on the redemption path is close to zero and the real thesis is acquisition.

IL.assessmentBasis: 35 ILCS 200/9-145: property outside Cook County is assessed at 33⅓% of fair cash value.

17031.basis: Cook County Classification Ordinance: Class 2 residential is assessed at 10% of market value, not the statutory 33⅓%.

IL.statute: 35 ILCS 200, Art. 21 (sale and redemption); Art. 22 (tax deed)
caveats: The penalty is bid DOWN from an 18% ceiling, so the tiers above are a best case, not an expectation. Recorded Cook sales cleared at a 0% median and a 1.88% mean across 64,526 liens — price an Illinois lien on the acquisition thesis, not the interest.
Cook County assesses residential at ~10% of market value, not the statutory 33⅓%. The county override above handles this; parcels in other Illinois counties use the statutory ratio.

Title is perfected by petition for tax deed under Art. 22 rather than a classic quiet-title action. The cost and duration here are market practice for that proceeding plus any curative work an insurer requires, and are not fixed by statute.
Redemption runs 24 months for most property and 30 months only for an owner-occupied principal residence of 1–6 units. Commercial, industrial and vacant non-residential stay at 24.
Cook also runs a scavenger sale for long-delinquent parcels under different minimum-bid rules (35 ILCS 200/21-145 et seq.) that this entry does not model.

IN.assessmentBasis: Indiana assesses at 100% of true tax value (assessed value has equalled 100% of true tax value since the 2001 assessment year), so the statutory ratio is 1.0.
IN.derivedArvCaveat: Indiana's ratio is 1.0, but IC 6-1.1-31-6(c) says in terms that true tax value DOES NOT mean fair market value — it means market value-in-use, the value of the parcel for its current use. On a derelict or under-used parcel, which is most of what reaches a tax sale, value-in-use can sit well below what the land would fetch redeveloped, and on special-purpose property it can sit above. A 1.0 ratio here is not a licence to treat the assessment as an appraisal; get comparable sales.
IN.statute: IC 6-1.1-24 (sale of real property when taxes delinquent); IC 6-1.1-25 (redemption and tax deeds); IC 6-1.1-31-6 (true tax value)
caveats: THE PENALTY BASE IS THE MINIMUM BID, NOT YOUR BID. 110%/115% under IC 6-1.1-25-2 is computed on the minimum bid; the amount you paid above it earns only 5% per annum, and only for sales after 2014-06-30. Indiana sells by premium bidding, so on any competitive parcel the modelled tier overstates the return — a $1,200 minimum taken at $6,000 returns 10% on $1,200 and 5%/yr on $4,800, not 10% on $6,000. Treat the computed penalty as a ceiling until the type carries a penalty base.

THREE REDEMPTION REGIMES AND THIS ROW ENCODES ONE. IC 6-1.1-25-4(a): one year at an ordinary county tax sale; 120 days where the county executive holds the lien and the certificate went unsold, or on sale to a qualified purchasing agency; and NO redemption at all for a parcel on the county auditor's vacant-and-abandoned list under IC 6-1.1-24-1.5. Establish which applies before trusting the hold period — a vacant-and-abandoned parcel is effectively a deed sale.

Redemption also repays every subsequent tax, special assessment, interest, penalty and fee the purchaser paid after the sale, so carrying taxes during the redemption year is recoverable rather than sunk — but only if the parcel is in fact redeemed.

Commissioners' certificate sales under IC 6-1.1-24-6.1 sell previously unsold parcels at a discounted minimum bid set by the county executive, advertised three consecutive weeks at least thirty days ahead. Cheaper entry, 120-day redemption, and generally the parcels nobody wanted at the regular sale.

A tax deed is not a marketable title. After redemption lapses the purchaser must petition the court under IC 6-1.1-25-4.6, having given the notices required by IC 6-1.1-25-4.5; defective notice is the usual ground on which an Indiana tax deed is later attacked.
If the parcel sells above the minimum bid and is NOT redeemed, the former owner may claim the tax sale surplus. That money is not the purchaser's and should never be modelled as recoverable.
quietTitle costs here are a placeholder and have not been reviewed by the operator. Do not rely on a computed Indiana max bid until they are set.

KS.assessmentBasis: Kansas Constitution art. 11, § 1: real property is assessed uniformly by subclass — residential including multi-family at 11.5%, vacant lots 12%, not-for-profit 12%, commercial and industrial 25%, land devoted to agricultural use 30% of agricultural income value, public utility 33%, and all other urban and rural real property 30%. This entry uses the 11.5% residential rate.
KS.derivedArvCaveat: Kansas assesses by subclass and this entry assumes residential at 11.5%. Vacant lots at 12% are close enough not to matter. Commercial and industrial at 25% and the 'all other' residual at 30% are not: dividing by 0.115 overstates those by roughly 2.2x and 2.6x — the dangerous direction, and 'all other' is a residual that catches more than its name suggests. Agricultural land is assessed at 30% of agricultural income value rather than of market value at all, so a derived ARV there is meaningless. Check the subclass on the appraiser's record before bidding on anything that is not plainly a house or a vacant lot.
KS.statute: K.S.A. 79-2801 et seq. (judicial foreclosure and sale by county), 79-2401a (redemption while held by the county), 79-2804b (twelve-month action to set aside); Kan. Const. art. 11, § 1 (assessment subclasses)
caveats: TWELVE MONTHS OF TITLE RISK AFTER THE SALE, AND IT PAYS NOTHING. K.S.A. 79-2804b allows an action to open, vacate, modify or set aside the judgment or order of sale within twelve months of confirmation. It is a defect window, not a redemption — the purchaser earns no penalty for waiting it out, so unlike a redeemable-deed state the wait is pure carry.

YOU DO NOT OWN IT AT THE HAMMER. Title passes on the court's confirmation of the sale, not at the auction. Before confirmation there is no right to possession and no right to collect rent, which matters if the parcel is tenanted.

The redemption is spent before you bid. K.S.A. 79-2401a holds county-bid real estate subject to redemption for one year if abandoned, two for general non-homestead property and three for a homestead; the judicial foreclosure follows only after that, and the last chance to redeem is 5pm the day before the sheriff's sale.

Assessment is by constitutional subclass, not county: 11.5% residential, 12% vacant lots and not-for-profit, 25% commercial and industrial, 30% all other urban and rural, 33% public utility. Agricultural land is assessed on agricultural income value rather than market value.
Proceeds above the judgment go to the former owner, so a premium is not recoverable equity — Kansas already did what Tyler v. Hennepin County later required of other states.
quietTitle costs here are a placeholder and have not been reviewed by the operator. Do not rely on a computed Kansas max bid until they are set.

KY.assessmentBasis: Section 172 of the Kentucky Constitution requires all non-exempt property to be assessed at 100% of fair cash value — the price it would bring at a fair voluntary sale — as of 1 January (see also KRS 132.190).
KY.derivedArvCaveat: Kentucky assesses at 100% of fair cash value, so the ratio is honestly 1.0 — but that is the PVA's opinion of value as of 1 January of the assessment year, not an appraisal of this parcel today. Treat a derived ARV as a starting point and get comparable sales before bidding.
KY.statute: KRS Chapter 134 (certificates of delinquency: §§ 134.015, 134.119, 134.125-134.131, 134.420, 134.452, 134.490, 134.546); KRS 426.530 (post-sale redemption)
caveats: Kentucky sells LIENS, not deeds. The expected outcome is the taxpayer satisfying the certificate at 12% per annum, not acquiring the property. Ownership requires a separate judicial foreclosure at additional legal cost, and the maths above treats that cost as if it were quiet title.

THE ADVERTISED PARCEL COUNT OVERSTATES WHAT IS BUYABLE. A third-party purchaser already holding a prior-year certificate on a parcel has first priority, submits a priority list up to ten days before the sale, and every certificate allocated that way is REMOVED from the annual sale (KRS 134.128). On a large county roll a material share of the advertised certificates never reaches open bidding, so an announced count is an upper bound on availability, not inventory.

SECOND REDEMPTION THIS ROW CANNOT EXPRESS. If a foreclosure sale brings less than two-thirds of the appraised value, KRS 426.530 gives the defendant six months from the day of sale to redeem at the purchase money plus 10% per annum plus the purchaser's reasonable post-sale costs. Six months is the current text, amended effective 2016-07-15; older summaries say a year. Bidding above two-thirds of appraisal is what extinguishes this right.

ONE-YEAR TOLLING PERIOD. No action may be brought on a certificate until one year after the taxes became delinquent (1 January), and none at all after eleven years (KRS 134.546). A July purchase therefore sits roughly six months before enforcement can even begin.

Premium-bid sale. The opening figure is taxes, penalties, interest and administrative costs, and bidders bid the price UP; the 12% accrues on the amount paid to the clerk, so a premium is not dead money, but it does lower the effective yield against the certificate's face.

You cannot cherry-pick. Certificates are sold in lots whose size is set by the size of the county's roll — up to 5 for rolls under 500, rising to 50 for rolls of 2,500-7,500, and 2% of the roll per round beyond that — with selection order set by a random drawing at the start of the sale (103 KAR 5:180).

Registration is mandatory and volume triggers obligations. Participants register with the county clerk at least a week ahead; anyone paying more than five certificates statewide, more than three in one county, or more than $10,000 statewide in a calendar year must also register with the Department of Revenue and must offer delinquent taxpayers a monthly installment plan (KRS 134.128; 134.129; 134.490).

Notice duties are continuing, not one-off. Within 50 days of delivery the purchaser must notify the taxpayer by first-class mail with proof of mailing, must repeat that notice at least annually until an action is instituted, and must give 45 days' notice before instituting one (KRS 134.490). These are carrying costs and a source of title risk if missed.

Home-rule cities can differ. Kentucky grants broad home rule under KRS 82.082, and first-class city procedure sits in KRS Chapter 91 rather than Chapter 134. Confirm the selling entity in Louisville and Lexington before assuming county clerk procedure.

quietTitle costs here are a placeholder and have not been reviewed by the operator, and they stand for a judicial foreclosure rather than a quiet title suit. Do not rely on a computed Kentucky max bid until they are set.

redemption.extendedFor: three years from recordation for most property; blighted or abandoned property redeems in eighteen months

LA.assessmentBasis: La. Const. art. VII, § 18: land is assessed at 10% of fair market value, improvements for residential purposes at 10%, and other property at 15%. This entry uses the 10% residential rate.
LA.derivedArvCaveat: Louisiana assesses land and residential improvements at 10% and 'other property' at 15%. On a commercial parcel actually assessed at 15%, dividing by 0.10 overstates value by half — the dangerous direction. The homestead exemption also removes a slice of assessed value on an owner-occupied home, so a bare assessed figure there understates the property. Check the classification and whether a homestead exemption is in force before treating a derived ARV as a valuation.
LA.statute: La. R.S. 47:2151 et seq. as rewritten by Acts 774 and 557 of 2024, effective 2026-01-01 (tax lien auctions; R.S. 47:2154 time and price); La. Const. art. VII, §§ 18 (assessment), 25 (tax sales and redemption)
caveats: THE SYSTEM CHANGED ON 2026-01-01 AND MOST WRITING ABOUT LOUISIANA IS NOW WRONG. Acts 774 and 557 of 2024 replaced the ownership bid-down sale with a tax lien certificate auction. 'Tax sale title' is repealed, no adjudicated property is created after that date, and a bidder no longer ends up owning an undivided percentage of a house. Any guide, course or comparable sale predating 2026 describes the old mechanism.

THE RATE IS BID DOWN, AND THIS ROW ENCODES THE FLOOR. Bidding opens at 1% per month, moves in tenths of a percent, and no bid may reduce it below 0.7% per month. The tier is 8.4% a year — the floor, annualised — so a realised certificate pays between that and 12%. Modelling the 12% opening rate would repeat the Illinois error of quoting a ceiling as an expectation.
A FLAT 5% PENALTY IS ALSO DUE ON REDEMPTION and is not in the tier, which holds one number. It is not bid down, so it accrues whatever the auction does to the rate.

NO OBSERVED CLEARING DATA EXISTS. The market is months old; there is no Louisiana equivalent of the Cook County catalogue behind the Illinois entry. The floor makes the downside knowable, not the expectation. Treat the realised rate as unknown within 8.4%-12% until sales are recorded.

Redemption is three years from recordation, or eighteen months for blighted or abandoned property. The shorter period began as a New Orleans rule and was extended by constitutional amendment; confirm it applies in the parish in question. The period is peremptive but can be extended where required notice was not given, so a defective notice keeps the owner's right alive.
Louisiana has parishes, not counties, and Orleans has historically run its own procedure. Confirm the collector and the local rules before assuming a statewide process.

quietTitle costs here are a placeholder and have not been reviewed by the operator, and they price a suit under a statute the courts have not yet interpreted. Do not rely on a computed Louisiana max bid until they are set.

MA.assessmentBasis: M.G.L. c. 59, § 38 requires assessment at full and fair cash valuation, with no classification ratio applied to the assessed value. The Department of Revenue certifies each municipality's values on a five-year cycle, with interim-year adjustments between certifications.
MA.derivedArvCaveat: The ratio is 1.0 and the assessment is reasonably current, so a derived Massachusetts ARV is sound as a market figure. What it does not describe is what the investor gets. Since § 64A the excess equity above the tax title balance belongs to the former owner, so the ARV is not the upside — it is the number that determines how much of somebody else's money passes through the holder's escrow account. Use it to judge whether the position will be redeemed, not what it is worth if it is not.
MA.statute: M.G.L. c. 60, §§ 52-54 (taking and assignment of tax title), 62 (redemption at 8%), 64 (Land Court jurisdiction; excess equity preserved), 64A (election to retain or sell, sale procedure, excess equity), 65 (petition to foreclose after 12 months); c. 59, § 38 (full and fair cash valuation)
caveats: THE RATE WAS HALVED IN 2024. M.G.L. c. 60, § 62 now pays "interest at 8 per cent" where it paid 16%. Every Massachusetts yield figure in circulation predates the change and is double the truth. Municipalities may also waive interest entirely and offer repayment plans of five to ten years, so even 8% is a ceiling on what a given position collects.

THE EQUITY IS NOT THE INVESTOR'S ANY MORE. Under § 64A the judgment holder must elect within thirty days of final judgment to retain or sell, follow a prescribed appraisal and auction procedure, and pay the former owner the excess equity — gross proceeds less the tax title balance at judgment and the documented costs of sale — holding it meanwhile in a segregated interest-bearing account. § 64 preserves that right expressly against the foreclosure judgment. Massachusetts is an 8% instrument; do not underwrite it on taking the property.

THE REDEMPTION WINDOW HAS NO END, AND THE HOLDER CANNOT START THE CLOCK FOR A YEAR. § 65 permits a petition to foreclose only "after 12 months from the sale or taking" — earlier only where a municipality faces abandoned buildings or costs exceeding value — and nothing terminates the right of redemption until the Land Court does. The 1095 days in the tier is a modelling assumption for a typical cycle, not a statutory cap. A position can run considerably longer, earning 8% throughout.

WHAT IS BOUGHT IS A TAX TITLE, NOT A DEED. Massachusetts municipalities take title for unpaid taxes and may assign the tax title; the assignee holds a lien interest that becomes ownership only through the Land Court, which has exclusive jurisdiction. The quietTitle field here holds the cost of that foreclosure, which is mandatory rather than optional.
quietTitle costs here are a placeholder and have not been reviewed by the operator, and in this state they are a core cost of every deal rather than a contingency.

MI.assessmentBasis: Michigan state equalized value is 50% of true cash value by constitution (Mich. Const. art. IX, § 3); taxable value may be lower still. The SEV published with these auction listings is taken from the delinquent tax year that was foreclosed upon, so it is typically several years stale — in a rising market it understates current value, and in a falling one it overstates it.
MI.statute: MCL 211.78 et seq. (general property tax act, foreclosure)
caveats: Michigan's foreclosure judgment cuts off prior liens and the owner's interest, so title is comparatively clean — quiet title is often unnecessary.
Valuations here derive from a stale SEV, not comps. Treat the computed ARV as a starting point and override it with real comparable sales before bidding at the ceiling.
Rand v. Rand / Hall-era excess-proceeds rules mean former owners may claim surplus; this does not affect the buyer's title.

MN.assessmentBasis: Minn. Stat. § 273.11 subd. 1: "all property shall be valued at its market value." Class rates under § 273.13 are applied afterwards to compute tax capacity and do not reduce the assessed value. The estimated market value is also what § 282.005 uses to set the opening price at a tax-forfeited sale.
MN.derivedArvCaveat: The ratio is 1.0 because the assessor's estimated market value is already a market figure, so a derived Minnesota ARV is only as good as the last assessment. It is the same number the county opened the auction at, which means a parcel that failed to sell at its EMV has been rejected by the market at exactly the value this ARV asserts — read a no-sale as evidence about the number, not just about the parcel.
MN.statute: Minn. Stat. §§ 281.17 (redemption period), 281.18 (absolute title vests in the state), 282.005 (initial sale of tax-forfeited land, excess proceeds), 282.01 (classification and sale), 273.11 (valuation at market value), 429.071 subd. 4 (reassessment of cancelled special assessments); Laws 2024, ch. 127, art. 70
caveats: THE SAME PARCEL HAS TWO PRICES THIRTY DAYS APART, AND THE SECOND IS THE TAX BILL. Under § 282.005 the initial price is "equal to the estimated market value, as determined by the most recent assessment", and "the property must not be sold for less than the initial price for 30 days after it is initially made available at auction". Then: "if no buyer is willing to pay the initial price, the price for the property must be reduced to the minimum bid" — the sum of delinquent taxes, special assessments, penalties, interest and costs. A Minnesota listing is worth almost nothing at market value and potentially a great deal at the tax debt, and the engine cannot tell which stage an opening bid represents. Establish that before treating a Minnesota figure as real.

CANCELLED SPECIAL ASSESSMENTS CAN COME BACK ON THE BUYER. § 429.071 subd. 4: "When a parcel of tax-forfeited land is returned to private ownership and the parcel is benefited by an improvement for which special assessments were canceled because of the forfeiture, the municipality that made the improvement may ... make a reassessment or a new assessment as to the parcel in an amount equal to the amount remaining unpaid on the original assessment." Forfeiture wipes the assessment and the sale can revive it. This is parcel-specific, can run to thousands on improved land, and is not in closingCosts.

Redemption runs three years from the tax judgment sale to the state (§ 281.17), but one year for non-homesteaded land in a targeted community and for qualified waste disposal facilities. All of it expires before the parcel reaches auction, so it affects when inventory appears, not what a buyer earns.

Surplus above the minimum bid belongs to the former owner and other interested parties, not the county — the point of the 2024 rewrite. The auditor notifies within 60 days and claimants have six months to file. This does not affect the buyer's title or price, but it means a Minnesota county has no revenue reason to push the price above the tax debt.

If nobody pays even the minimum bid, "the state is deemed to have purchased the property through a credit bid" and the parcel is disposed of under the rest of chapter 282. A parcel can therefore leave the auction calendar without a private sale having happened.

MO.assessmentBasis: RSMo 137.115(5)(1) assesses real property by subclass as a percentage of true value in money: residential 19%, agricultural and horticultural 12%, and utility, industrial, commercial and all other 32%. This entry uses the residential rate.
MO.derivedArvCaveat: Missouri's three subclasses span 12% to 32%, so the classification matters more than the number. Dividing a commercial assessment by the residential 0.19 overstates the property by about 1.7x, the dangerous direction. Dividing an agricultural assessment by 0.19 understates it by about a third — safe, but it will make farmland look worthless. Confirm the subclass on the assessor's record before accepting a derived Missouri value.
MO.statute: RSMo §§ 140.150 et seq. (Jones-Munger tax certificate sales), 140.340 (redemption within one year, up to 10%), 140.405 (title search, ninety-day notice to owner and lienholders, forfeiture for non-compliance), 140.250 (subsequent offerings); § 137.115 (assessment subclasses). Chapter 141 governs St. Louis City and Jackson County separately.
caveats: A NOTICE FAILURE FORFEITS THE ENTIRE INVESTMENT, NOT JUST THE DEED. RSMo 140.405: "Failure of the purchaser to comply with this section shall result in such purchaser's loss of all interest in the real estate." Compliance means a title search report from a licensed attorney or title company, notice to the owner and every recorded lienholder at least ninety days before the deed may be taken, sent by both first class and certified mail, and an affidavit filed with the collector. Budget the title search and the mailings as certain costs of every Missouri position, and treat the ninety-day deadline as the hardest date in this file.

THE 10% IS A CEILING SET BY THE CERTIFICATE. § 140.340 pays "interest at the rate specified in such certificate, not to exceed ten percent annually", plus eight per cent on subsequent taxes the holder pays. The tier is the ceiling; read the certificate before assuming it.

SUBSEQUENT OFFERINGS ARE A DIFFERENT INSTRUMENT. A parcel unsold at its first offering is offered again, and the terms — price, redemption and the deed timetable — change with the offering number under § 140.250. Nothing in a listing necessarily says which offering it is, and this entry models a first-offering certificate.

ST. LOUIS CITY AND JACKSON COUNTY DO NOT USE THIS CHAPTER. They operate under chapter 141, the land tax collection act, which is a court-supervised process with different timing and a different deed. A parcel in either is not priced by this entry.

MS.assessmentBasis: Miss. Const. art. 4, § 112: Class I, single-family owner-occupied residential, is assessed at 10% of true value; Class II, all other real property, at 15%; Class III at 15% and Class IV public utility property at 30%. This entry uses the Class II rate.
MS.derivedArvCaveat: Section 112 also requires that "in arriving at the true value of Class I and Class II property, the appraisal shall be made according to current use, regardless of location". Mississippi does not assess real property at its highest and best use — it assesses what is there now, so a vacant or derelict parcel on valuable ground is carried at the value of the vacancy. A derived Mississippi ARV therefore understates redevelopment potential by design rather than by lag, and no amount of recency in the assessment will fix it. Class also matters: at 0.15 an owner-occupied Class I parcel is understated by a third, which is the safe direction but will make a house look like a lot.
MS.statute: Miss. Code Ann. §§ 27-41-55 and 27-41-59 (annual sale, conduct and online bidding), 27-41-77 (disposition of excess bid), 27-43-3 (notice before expiry of redemption; sale void for failure), 27-45-3 (redemption, 5% damages, 1.5% per month), 27-45-23 (chancery clerk's conveyance); Miss. Const. art. 4, § 112 (classes and assessment rates)
caveats: A COUNTY CLERK'S MISTAKE VOIDS THE SALE, AND THE CLERK IS NOT LIABLE. § 27-43-3 requires the chancery clerk to notify the owner at least forty-five days before the redemption period expires, by personal service or service at the abode, by registered or certified mail, and by publication. Then: "Should the clerk inadvertently fail to send notice as prescribed in this section, then the sale shall be void and the clerk shall not be liable to the purchaser or owner upon refund of all purchase money paid." The purchase money comes back; the position, the two years of accrued interest and the deal do not, and nothing the investor does can prevent it. Mississippi tax sales are voided on this ground routinely.

THE OVERBID IS A DEAD LOSS AND EARNS NOTHING. Mississippi bids up from the face amount, and the 5% damages and 1.5% monthly interest under § 27-45-3 run on "all such taxes and costs" — not on the premium. If the owner redeems, § 27-41-77 keeps the excess with the county rather than returning it. So a bidder who pays a 40% premium has turned an 18% instrument into roughly 13% and forfeited the premium outright. The tier is the statutory rate on the face amount, not the yield on the money spent.

A FLAT 5% SITS ON TOP OF THE 18%. § 27-45-3 adds "five percent (5%) damages" on the amount of taxes, separately from the monthly interest. The tier holds one number and cannot carry both, so the 5% is not in the computed return.

TWO YEARS IS A LONG TIME TO BE RIGHT ABOUT. Redemption runs the full two years from the day of sale before any deed exists, and auctionToMarketableMonths reflects that plus the action to clear title. Mississippi is the slowest lien in this file after Wyoming.

COUNTIES SELL ON TWO DIFFERENT DATES. Most hold the sale on the last Monday in August; the rest on the first Monday in April. A state-level calendar that assumes one date will miss half the inventory, and the state disappears from any forward-looking view for most of the year.

Excess bid goes to the former owner on request once redemption expires, and to the county if unclaimed after two more years (§ 27-41-77), so Mississippi is not exposed on the Tyler v. Hennepin question.

NC.assessmentBasis: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 105-283 requires all property to be appraised at its true value in money, which the statute defines as market value. There is no classification ratio and no county variation in the ratio itself — only in how recently it was measured.
NC.derivedArvCaveat: North Carolina has the longest reappraisal cycle in the country. G.S. 105-286(a)(1) requires each county to reappraise "as of January 1 of the year set out in the following schedule and every eighth year thereafter", so an assessment can be eight years old and still current by law. Only counties of 75,000 or more face an earlier trigger, and only when their sales assessment ratio drifts out of bounds. A derived North Carolina ARV is a market value as of a date that may predate the last cycle of the market entirely — treat it as the weakest derived figure in this file and override it with comparable sales wherever the number matters.
NC.statute: N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 105-374 (mortgage-style foreclosure, upset bids, title), 105-375 (in rem foreclosure and execution sale), 105-283 (true value in money), 105-286 (octennial reappraisal), 105-277.4 (present-use value deferral and rollback); G.S. 1-339.25 and 1-339.64 (upset bids)
caveats: THE MAX BID IS A WALK-AWAY PRICE, NOT AN OPENING BID, AND NORTH CAROLINA WILL TEST IT. Any sale can be upset within ten days by 5% or $750, whichever is greater, and each upset restarts the ten days. Bidding the computed ceiling at the auction leaves nowhere to go when someone raises it, and matching the raise puts the operator past the ceiling. Bid low, expect to be upset, and treat the computed figure as the point at which to stop — in this state, uniquely, that discipline is enforced by the process rather than left to the bidder.

THE TIMELINE HAS NO FIXED END. Confirmation cannot be applied for until ten days pass with no exception or increased bid, and a determined underbidder can extend that indefinitely in ten-day increments for $750 a time. Deposits are tied up throughout. auctionToMarketableMonths assumes this resolves in roughly two months; a contested parcel will take longer.

SOME TAX LIENS SURVIVE, BY NAME. G.S. 105-375 conveys fee simple free and clear "except the liens of other taxes or special assessments not paid from the purchase price and not included in the judgment, liens arising from C-PACE assessments authorized under Article 10B of Chapter 160A of the General Statutes, and conservation agreements". A tax year outside the judgment stays with the parcel, and C-PACE — commercial energy financing, repaid through the tax bill — can be a large balance that survives specifically because it is not an ordinary lien.

FARM AND FOREST LAND CARRIES THREE YEARS OF DEFERRED TAX THAT THE BUYER CAN TRIGGER. Land classified at present-use value under G.S. 105-277.4 is taxed on its use rather than its market value, and on a disqualifying event "the deferred taxes for the preceding three fiscal years are due and payable", as a lien on the property under G.S. 105-355(a). Changing the use is the disqualifying event, so the act that realises the value also crystallises the bill. A derived ARV from a present-use assessment also badly understates the parcel.

NM.assessmentBasis: NMSA 1978, § 7-37-3: taxable value is one third (33⅓%) of the net taxable value of the property. New Mexico applies this uniformly statewide rather than by class or county.
NM.derivedArvCaveat: The ratio is honest, but NMSA 1978, § 7-36-21.2 caps annual increases in the valuation of residential property at 3%, so a long-held home's assessed value can sit well below market — the California Proposition 13 problem under a different statute. The cap is removed when the property changes ownership, so a recently transferred parcel tracks market far more closely than one held for decades. Get comparable sales before treating a ratio-derived ARV as a valuation.
NM.statute: NMSA 1978, §§ 7-38-65 (sale of real property for delinquent taxes), 7-38-70 (deeds; effect; two-year limitation on challenge); § 7-37-3 (taxable value); § 7-36-21.2 (residential valuation cap)
caveats: THE DEED IS SUBJECT TO EARLIER PERFECTED INTERESTS. § 7-38-70 conveys the former owner's interest as of the date the tax lien arose, 'subject only to perfected interests in the real property existing before' that date. A mortgage or judgment perfected before the lien arose survives the sale. Establish the lien date and search back from it before treating survivingLiens as zero.

TWO YEARS OF CHALLENGE RISK THAT PAYS NOTHING. The former owner, or anyone claiming through them, is barred from challenging the conveyance only after two years from the date of sale. That is a defect window rather than a redemption — no penalty accrues to the purchaser for waiting it out, so it is pure carry.

THE STATE SELLS, NOT THE COUNTY. Sales are conducted by the Property Tax Division of the Taxation and Revenue Department under § 7-38-65, which may sell at any time after three years from the first delinquency date. Procedure, notice and catalogue are the Division's, not each county's.

Residential valuations are capped at 3% growth a year (§ 7-36-21.2) and the cap lifts on a change of ownership, so assessed value understates market on long-held homes and tracks it on recently transferred ones. Two parcels of identical worth can carry very different assessments.

NV.assessmentBasis: NRS 361.225 fixes the assessment ratio at 35% of taxable value for all property. NRS 361.227 determines taxable value as the full cash value of the land plus the replacement cost of improvements less depreciation, where depreciation runs at 1.5% of replacement cost for each year of adjusted actual age up to a maximum of 50 years.
NV.derivedArvCaveat: Nevada's 35% is applied to taxable value, which for improved property is not market value and is not trying to be. Improvements are valued at replacement cost less 1.5% a year of depreciation up to fifty years, so a fifty-year-old building is carried at a quarter of what it would cost to rebuild, regardless of what it would sell for. Dividing an assessment on an older improved parcel by 0.35 therefore returns something well below market — the safe direction, but wrong enough to make a sound deal look impossible. The distortion grows with the age of the structure and is absent on bare land, where taxable value is full cash value.
NV.statute: NRS §§ 361.567 and 361.570 (trustee's certificate; two-year period, one year if abandoned), 361.585 (deed in trust to the county treasurer; reconveyance), 361.595 (conveyance to purchasers), 361.603 (90-day reconveyance period), 361.610 (disposition of proceeds); NRS 361.225 (rate of assessment), 361.227 (determination of taxable value)
caveats: THE ASSESSMENT IS NOT A FRACTION OF MARKET VALUE. Nevada's 35% applies to taxable value, and NRS 361.227 builds taxable value for improvements from replacement cost less 1.5% per year of age, capped at fifty years. On an older house that is a construction-cost figure with three-quarters written off, not a sale price. Treat a derived Nevada ARV on improved property as a floor and override it with comparable sales; on vacant land, where taxable value is full cash value, the derivation is sound.

ABANDONED PROPERTY MOVES TWICE AS FAST. Where a property is determined abandoned under NRS 361.567 the treasurer holds it for one year rather than two, so Nevada inventory can reach sale in half the usual time — and an abandoned determination is also a statement about the condition of what is being sold.

The former owner gets one more chance than in most states. After the treasurer's deed in trust, reconveyance remains available for the 90-day period in NRS 361.603 and until 5 p.m. on the third business day before the sale. A listed Nevada parcel can be withdrawn within days of the auction.

NY.assessmentBasis: New York has no statewide level of assessment. Each of 1,200+ assessing units sets its own, and ORPTS publishes an equalization rate and residential assessment ratio per unit each year. 1.0 is used here as a deliberate floor — see the derived-ARV note — not as a claim that New York assesses at full value.
NY.derivedArvCaveat: DO NOT TRADE OFF A DERIVED ARV IN NEW YORK. Levels of assessment range from a few percent of market value to 100% across more than 1,200 assessing units, and this entry assumes 100% precisely because that is the end of the range that cannot cause an overbid. In a town assessing at 5%, a derived ARV understates the property twentyfold and the max bid will look absurdly low — that is the model refusing to guess, not the parcel being worthless. Look up the municipality's equalization rate or RAR, or supply arvOverride from comparable sales.
NY.statute: N.Y. Real Property Tax Law Article 11 (in rem tax foreclosure: §§ 1110 redemption, 1131 failure to redeem, 1136 judgment); L 2024, ch 55, pt BB (surplus proceeds)
caveats: THE ASSESSED VALUE IS NOT COMPARABLE ACROSS MUNICIPALITIES. More than 1,200 assessing units each set their own level of assessment, published annually by ORPTS as an equalization rate and a residential assessment ratio. This row assumes 100% as a deliberate floor, so a derived ARV in a low-assessing town is far too low. That is the safe direction, and it makes the derived figure useless as a valuation — get the municipality's rate or supply arvOverride.

NO REDEMPTION FOR THE AUCTION BUYER, AND THIS TIME THAT IS UNQUALIFIED. RPTL 1110's period runs before the tax district takes title; RPTL 1131 and 1136(3) bar the former owner on judgment. By the time a parcel reaches the county auction the right is gone. The default period is two years from the lien date and a district may set a longer one, but either way it expires pre-auction.

SURPLUS NOW GOES BACK TO THE FORMER OWNER. L 2024, ch 55, pt BB amended Article 11 after Tyler v. Hennepin County so excess proceeds are returned to the former owner and, where appropriate, to lienors. This does not change what a bidder pays, but it removes the county's old incentive to retain equity and is worth understanding before assuming how a district will run its sale.

NOT EVERY NEW YORK TAX SALE IS AN ARTICLE 11 COUNTY AUCTION. New York City and several cities have run their own tax lien certificate programmes under separate authority, which are different instruments with different economics. Confirm the selling entity and the enabling law before applying this row.

OH.assessmentBasis: R.C. 5715.01: taxable value is the percentage of true value the tax commissioner sets by rule, capped at 35%. The rule has been at the 35% ceiling for decades and applies uniformly statewide, with no classification by property type and no county overrides.
OH.derivedArvCaveat: Farmland enrolled in Ohio's CAUV programme is assessed on its current agricultural use value rather than market value (R.C. 5713.31), and the two differ by an order of magnitude on development-fringe land. Dividing a CAUV assessment by 0.35 returns roughly the agricultural value, not what the parcel would sell for — it understates, which is the safe direction, but it makes a genuinely valuable parcel look worthless. Most of the Ohio inventory sits in rural counties where enrolment is common, so check the auditor's record for a CAUV flag before accepting a low derived ARV.
OH.statute: R.C. 5721.18-5721.20 (tax foreclosure and sheriff's sale), 5721.25 (redemption before confirmation), 5723.06 (auditor's sale of forfeited land), 5723.13 (one-year bar on contesting title), 5715.01 (assessment); tax certificates, not priced here, at 5721.30-5721.43
caveats: THE FIRST SALE HAS A MARKET-VALUE FLOOR, WHICH IS WHY MOST OHIO PARCELS SHOW NO BID ROOM. R.C. 5721.19(A) lets the court order a parcel sold "without appraisal, for not less than either of the following: (1) The fair market value of the parcel, as determined by the county auditor, plus the costs incurred in the foreclosure proceeding" — or the total of the finding plus costs. Where the court picks the first, the minimum bid is market value and there is no discount to win. A max bid below the opening bid is the statute working, not a data error.

THE DISCOUNT LIVES IN THE SECOND OFFER. A parcel that fails at the judicial sale is forfeited to the state and offered by the auditor under R.C. 5723.06; if it fails there too, "the auditor may offer such tract for sale forthwith, and sell it for the best price obtainable" — no minimum at all. A listing described as a first offer, a forfeited land sale or an auditor's sale is a different economic proposition from a sheriff's sale, and the engine cannot tell them apart from the fields it has.

OHIO ALSO SELLS TAX CERTIFICATES AND THIS ENTRY DOES NOT PRICE THEM. Under R.C. 5721.32 bidding opens at 18% per year and steps down in quarter points "to the rate of zero per cent", with no floor — the New Jersey problem, and we have no observed clearing rate for Ohio. All current inventory is deed sales. Check the sale type before trusting an Ohio figure.

A federal tax lien properly filed before the foreclosure survives the sale, as do easements and covenants predating the delinquency (R.C. 5721.19(F)(2)). Everything else is extinguished at confirmation. Taxes levied but not yet due and payable are not part of the finding and stay with the parcel.

You cannot bid if you owe delinquent property tax anywhere in Ohio. R.C. 5721.19(J) requires the purchaser to furnish an affidavit that they have inquired of the county treasurers and own no Ohio property with delinquent taxes against it; the sheriff will not transfer title without it, and a false affidavit is falsification.

The conveyance fee is ad valorem and is not in closingCosts as a rate: $1 per $1,000 to the state under R.C. 319.54(G)(3), plus a permissive county fee of up to $3 per $1,000 under R.C. 322.02. On a $25,000 parcel that is $25 to $100. The flat figure here assumes a low-priced parcel; on an expensive one it understates.

The expedited land bank track under R.C. 323.65-323.79 transfers abandoned parcels to a land reutilization corporation by deed with no sale and no surplus, and the Sixth Circuit held in Hall v. Meisner, 51 F.4th 185 (6th Cir. 2022) that taking the owner's equity that way violates the Takings Clause. Ohio has not amended the statute in response — HB 375 of the 135th General Assembly would have let owners force a public sale and died in committee. This does not affect a buyer's title at a sale, but it removes inventory from the calendar before it is ever auctioned.

OR.assessmentBasis: Oregon has no statutory assessment ratio. Measure 50 (Or. Const. art. XI, § 11) set each property's maximum assessed value at 90% of its 1995-96 real market value and caps growth at 3% a year, so assessed value is the lesser of MAV and real market value and drifts below market over time. 0.536 is the statewide ratio of assessed value to real market value the Department of Revenue reports for FY 2025-26, up from 0.526 in FY 2024-25.

41001.basis: Baker County: assessed value $2,174,134k against Measure 5 value $3,670,343k, Oregon DOR Property Tax Statistics FY 2025-26, Exhibit 6a.

41039.basis: Lane County: assessed value $44,980,819k against Measure 5 value $87,659,683k, Oregon DOR Property Tax Statistics FY 2025-26, Exhibit 6a.

41047.basis: Marion County: assessed value $34,979,794k against Measure 5 value $63,756,395k, Oregon DOR Property Tax Statistics FY 2025-26, Exhibit 6a.

OR.derivedArvCaveat: Oregon county assessors publish BOTH a real market value and a Measure 50 assessed value for every parcel, and the ratio here converts the second into the first. If the figure captured for a parcel was already the real market value, dividing it by 0.536 inflates the property by about 1.9x — the single easiest way to get an Oregon number badly wrong, and it fails in the unsafe direction. Beyond that, 0.536 is a statewide aggregate and no individual parcel is the aggregate: a property that has not changed hands or been improved since 1995 sits far below it, while one recently built or partitioned is reassessed toward market and sits near 1.0. Treat a derived Oregon ARV as a starting point and check the assessor's own RMV, which is published.
OR.statute: ORS 312.010 (three years to foreclosure), 312.120 (two-year redemption, 5% penalty), 312.200 (deed to county, redemption terminates), 312.230 (two-year bar on challenges), 312.270 (title free of liens); ORS 275.110-275.200 (county resale); Or. Const. art. XI, § 11 (Measure 50)
caveats: THE ASSESSMENT RATIO IS AN OBSERVATION, NOT A LAW, AND IT MOVES EVERY YEAR. Oregon has no statutory ratio. The statewide figure went from 0.526 to 0.536 in one year because assessed values grew faster than market values, and it will move again when the Department of Revenue publishes the next report each summer. An asOf that has gone stale matters more here than in any other state in this file — elsewhere a stale date means a statute might have been amended, here it means the number is simply out of date.

THE COUNTY SETS THE MINIMUM PRICE AT ITS OWN DISCRETION AND CAN DROP IT TO 15%. ORS 275.110 has the governing body 'fix the minimum price' with no appraisal required, and the sheriff sells 'to the highest and best bidder' (ORS 275.190). If nothing sells, ORS 275.200(2) lets the county sell privately 'for not less than the largest amount bid for the land at the sheriff's sale, or, if no bid was made, at a price the governing body of the county deems reasonable, but at a price no less than 15 percent of the minimum bid'. A parcel on its second pass is a different proposition from one on its first, and neither the price nor the discount is set by statute.

Oregon counties may sell on installments of up to twenty years (ORS 275.190). A contract sale is not the cash purchase the engine models, and the parcel is not free to resell while the county holds the contract.

The county ratios cover only the three counties currently holding inventory — Baker, Lane and Marion. A parcel in any other Oregon county falls back to the statewide 0.536, which will be wrong in one direction or the other by several points.

Redemption is the owner's, not the investor's. The 5% penalty and interest under ORS 312.120 are paid to the county during the two years before it takes its deed. Nothing in an Oregon sale pays a return to the buyer for waiting, which is why redemption is null rather than a tier.

PA.derivedArvCaveat: Pennsylvania county assessments run against base years that can be decades stale, and the spread is extreme — Bucks assesses at about 5.6% of market and Schuylkill at 100%, an 18x range inside one state. The Common Level Ratio is a county MEDIAN published for realty transfer tax equalisation, not a per-parcel appraisal, so deriving ARV from it multiplies any error in that one parcel's assessment by the factor: in Bucks a $50,000 assessment derives an ARV near $893,000. Treat a derived ARV in a high-factor county as a research lead, not a valuation, and get comparable sales before bidding.
PA.statute: 72 P.S. §§ 5860.101-5860.803 (Real Estate Tax Sale Law); 53 P.S. §§ 7101-7505 (Municipal Claims and Tax Liens Act, Philadelphia and Allegheny)
caveats: UPSET SALE vs JUDICIAL SALE is the single most important distinction in Pennsylvania and this row cannot express it. An upset sale (72 P.S. §§ 5860.601-609) conveys subject to existing mortgages, judgments and liens, which are NOT divested; a judicial sale (§§ 5860.610-612) is ordered free and clear. Establish which one a parcel is in before treating survivingLiens as zero.

REALTY TRANSFER TAX IS NOT IN closingCosts. 61 Pa. Code § 91.193 excludes a conveyance to a local taxing authority acquiring at a tax claim bureau sale, and exempts a mortgage holder purchasing at judicial sale — it grants NO exclusion to a third-party purchaser. A third-party investor should expect 1% state plus local transfer tax (commonly 1%, and about 3.278% in Philadelphia) on the price. On a $50,000 parcel that is roughly $1,000 outside Philadelphia and materially more inside it. The engine has no percentage field for this; budget it manually.

PHILADELPHIA HAS A REDEMPTION AND THIS ROW SAYS IT DOES NOT. Under MCTLA 53 P.S. § 7293 an owner-occupied property (occupancy determined 90 days before the sale) may be redeemed within nine months of acknowledgment of the sheriff's deed, at the price paid plus 10% per annum. Non-owner-occupied and abandoned property carries no such right. Modelling that here would apply it to the 65 RETSL counties that lack it, so it is recorded as a caveat and the redemption field stays null — conservative for return, but it means the engine does not warn about redemption risk on a Philadelphia parcel.
Allegheny County also runs under MCTLA rather than RETSL, so its procedure and notice rules differ from the other 65 counties.
Common Level Ratios are re-published by STEB every year and take effect each 1 July. The figures here are the 2025 CLR set effective 2026-07-01 to 2027-06-30; re-verify after the next July.

Philadelphia's CLR factor is 1.06 for documents accepted 2026-07-01 through 2026-12-31 and 1.00 after 2026-12-31, following an assessment base change. The ratio recorded here (0.9434) is the former; it becomes 1.00 on 2027-01-01.

In high-CLR-factor counties (Bucks 17.86, Butler 16.67, Franklin 13.89, Juniata 13.51, Westmoreland 11.49, Pike 11.24, Northumberland 10.53) a derived ARV is amplified roughly 11-18x from the assessment. Do not bid off a ratio-derived ARV in those counties; supply arvOverride from comparable sales.

RETSL requires publication, posting and certified mail notice, and an owner-occupied property cannot be sold unless the owner was personally served at least ten days before the sale. Defective notice is the most common ground on which Pennsylvania tax sales are set aside, which is a risk to the purchaser's title rather than to the price.

SC.assessmentBasis: S.C. Code § 12-43-220(e): all other real property not otherwise provided for is assessed at six percent of fair market value. South Carolina assesses by property class rather than by county — 4% legal residence (c), 4% agricultural held by individuals (d)(1)(A), 6% agricultural held by corporations (d)(1)(B), 10.5% manufacturing and utility (a)(1).
SC.derivedArvCaveat: South Carolina's ratio depends on the property's CLASS, and this entry uses the 6% residual. A parcel actually carrying the 4% legal-residence ratio will have its ARV understated by a third here, which is the safe direction. A manufacturing or utility parcel assessed at 10.5% is the dangerous one: dividing by 0.06 overstates its value by roughly 1.75x. Confirm the class on the assessor's record before bidding on anything that is not ordinary residential or commercial land.
SC.statute: S.C. Code Title 12, Ch. 51 (alternate procedure for collection of property taxes: §§ 12-51-55, 12-51-90, 12-51-130); § 12-43-220 (assessment ratios)
caveats: THE PENALTY IS CAPPED AT THE OPENING BID. § 12-51-90 provides that interest due on redemption may not exceed the forfeited land commission's bid under § 12-51-55 — roughly taxes plus costs. The tiers above are therefore a ceiling reached only by a bid at or near the minimum; a purchase at several times the minimum collects the same capped sum, so the effective yield falls as the premium rises.

THE OVERAGE IS NOT YOURS. Under § 12-51-130 everything bid above taxes, assessments, penalties and costs belongs to the owner of record immediately before the redemption period ended, payable ninety days after the deed and escheating to the county only after five unclaimed years. A premium is not recoverable equity; South Carolina was already Tyler-compliant on this point.

Assessment is by class, not by county. This row uses the 6% residual under § 12-43-220(e); legal residences sit at 4% and manufacturing and utility property at 10.5%. See the derived-ARV note — the 10.5% case is the one that produces a dangerous overstatement.

The deed becomes incontestable on procedural or other grounds only after the twelve-month redemption period plus a further twelve months (§ 12-51-90). Before that, procedural defects in the sale remain a live attack on title.

Unsold parcels are bid in for the Forfeited Land Commission under § 12-51-55 rather than left unsold, which is also what sets the interest cap above. An FLC-held parcel is a different instrument from one bought at open auction.

TN.assessmentBasis: T.C.A. § 67-5-801 and Tenn. Const. art. II, § 28: residential and farm property is assessed at 25% of value, industrial and commercial at 40%, public utility at 55%. This entry uses the 25% residential rate.
TN.derivedArvCaveat: Tennessee assesses by class and this entry assumes residential at 25%. On an industrial or commercial parcel actually assessed at 40%, dividing by 0.25 overstates the property by about 1.6x — the dangerous direction. A mixed-use parcel is apportioned between subclasses by State Board of Equalization rules, so it will sit somewhere between. Check the class on the assessor's record before bidding on anything that is not plainly residential.
TN.statute: T.C.A. Title 67, ch. 5: §§ 67-5-2701 to 67-5-2703 (redemption), § 67-5-801 (classification and rate of assessment)
caveats: THE REDEMPTION PERIOD DEPENDS ON THE ARREARS, AND THIS ROW ENCODES THE LONGEST. One year at five years' delinquency or less, 180 days above five, 90 days at eight or more, and 30 days for property shown vacant or abandoned (§ 67-5-2701(a)(1)). A deeply delinquent parcel therefore returns capital far sooner than modelled — favourable, but it also means a shorter window in which the 12% accrues.

THE CLOCK STARTS AT THE ORDER CONFIRMING THE SALE, NOT THE SALE. Tennessee sells through the Chancery Court's Clerk and Master, and the period runs from confirmation. Money is committed from the auction; the redemption period begins later. Budget the gap separately — it is in auctionToMarketableMonths and cannot be in maxDays.

Interest accrues on the ENTIRE purchase price, not a minimum bid and not capped (§ 67-5-2701(b)(1)), and it runs from payment until the redemption motion is filed rather than to the end of the period. A premium here earns, unlike Indiana or South Carolina.

Redemption also repays delinquent taxes, penalty, interest and court costs, and the court may award the purchaser amounts expended on the property (§ 67-5-2701(e), (f), (j)). Those are recoverable only on redemption, not if the buyer keeps the parcel.

Assessment is by class, not county. This row assumes residential at 25%; commercial and industrial sit at 40% and public utility at 55%. See the derived-ARV note — the commercial case overstates value by roughly 1.6x.

VA.assessmentBasis: Va. Const. art. X, § 2: "All assessments of real estate and tangible personal property shall be at their fair market value, to be ascertained as prescribed by law." There is no classification and no ratio below full value, except the agricultural, horticultural, forest and open-space use-value deferral the same section authorises.
VA.derivedArvCaveat: Virginia assesses at full fair market value, so the ratio is honestly 1.0 — but it is the value as of the last general reassessment, not today. Counties reassess every four years, or every three by vote of the board, and a county of 50,000 or fewer may stretch to five- or six-year intervals (§ 58.1-3252). Most of the Virginia inventory sits in exactly those small counties, so an assessment here can be half a decade old in either direction. Agricultural, horticultural, forest and open-space land enrolled in use-value deferral is assessed on its use value rather than market value, which understates it sharply on development-fringe parcels. A 1.0 ratio is not a licence to treat the assessment as an appraisal.
VA.statute: Va. Code §§ 58.1-3965 to 58.1-3974 (judicial sale of tax-delinquent real estate), 58.1-3967 (parties defendant and effect on liens), 58.1-3975 (nonjudicial sale of low-value parcels), 58.1-3252 (reassessment cycle); Va. Const. art. X, § 2 (assessment at fair market value)
caveats: THE COMPUTED MAX BID IS AN ALL-IN CEILING AND VIRGINIA ADDS A BUYER'S PREMIUM ON TOP OF THE BID. Both sales in our own inventory charge one: Shenandoah County's judicial sale adds 10% of the high bid, and the City of Chesapeake's nonjudicial sale adds 15% plus a $200 recordation fee. Bid at most maxBid ÷ 1.10, or ÷ 1.15 where the terms say 15%. Bidding the computed figure itself overshoots the ceiling by the whole premium — on a $20,000 parcel that is $2,000 to $3,000 of profit that was never there. closingCosts is a flat dollar field and cannot hold a rate; read the auctioneer's terms for every sale.

AT A NONJUDICIAL SALE A PRIOR DEED OF TRUST CAN SURVIVE, AND THE LISTING WILL NOT SAY SO. § 58.1-3975 conveys free of the locality's tax lien "but shall not affect ... liens recorded prior to the date of sale unless the treasurer has given the lienholder written notice of the sale at least 30 days prior to the sale". Whether that notice went out is not on the public record. The Chesapeake terms in our own inventory advertise the parcels as "sold free and clear of liens & encumbrances", which is the auctioneer's phrasing and not what the statute says. Pull a title search before bidding on any nonjudicial parcel.

A JUDICIAL SALE IS THE STRONGER TITLE, BUT ONLY AS TO PARTIES SERVED. § 58.1-3967 frees the title of creditors' claims, "provided that such creditor, person, or entity was made a party defendant". A lienholder who was never named keeps their lien. The court file shows who was named, which is the whole advantage over the nonjudicial track.

NONJUDICIAL PARCELS ARE SMALL AND USUALLY UNBUILDABLE BY STATUTORY DESIGN. § 58.1-3975 reaches parcels assessed at $15,000 or less, or $15,001-$30,000 if unimproved and under an acre or unsuitable for building or condemned or derelict or blighted, or $30,001-$40,000 if in a revitalization zone, unimproved and under half an acre. A derived ARV can make one of these look like a house lot when the statute that put it in the sale says it is not.

Virginia localities are not all counties. Thirty-eight independent cities sit outside any county and levy their own tax — Chesapeake, Newport News, Suffolk, Danville, Martinsville and Portsmouth are all in the current inventory. Towns are a further layer: § 58.1-3974 makes a redeeming owner pay "any outstanding taxes, penalties, and interest owed to a town or other concurrent taxing entity", so a parcel can owe two governments and a county's sale does not necessarily clear the town's lien.

Virginia's recordation tax is ad valorem and is not in closingCosts. That figure is anchored on Chesapeake's flat $200 recordation fee plus clerk's recording; the state and local recordation tax scales with the price and is owed on top.

Surplus is the former owner's. At a nonjudicial sale "any excess proceeds shall remain the property of the former owner, subject to claims of creditors", escrowed for two years. This does not affect the buyer's title, but it means Virginia is not exposed on the Tyler v. Hennepin question.

VT.assessmentBasis: Vermont requires property to be listed at 100% of fair market value. The Department of Taxes publishes a Common Level of Appraisal for every town each year, measuring listed value against equalized fair market value, and a town's CLA is set to 100% in the year it reappraises. From FY26 a Statewide Adjustment — effectively the average level of appraisal for the whole state — is also applied to education tax rates.
VT.derivedArvCaveat: Vermont's real assessment ratio is the town's Common Level of Appraisal, not 1.0, and it is published per town rather than per county — Vermont has 246 towns and 14 counties, so it cannot be expressed in countyAssessmentRatios, which is keyed by county FIPS. Between reappraisals a town's listed values lag the market and the CLA falls below 100%, which makes a derived ARV at 1.0 conservative. The exception worth checking is a town that has just reappraised: its listed values jump to full market in a single year, and a parcel's assessment can rise sharply without the property changing at all.
VT.statute: 32 V.S.A. §§ 5252 (extension of warrant), 5260 (redemption, one per cent per month), 5261 (collector's deed); Act 73 of 2025 (minimum $1,500 delinquency), Act 106 of 2024 (repayment plans, notice, surplus-equity working group), Act 182 (no sale while a VHAP application is pending)
caveats: THE DEED REMAINDER IS THE RETURN HERE, AND IT IS THE PART UNDER REVIEW. If nobody redeems, the purchaser keeps a property worth far more than the tax debt, with no obligation to pay the former owner the difference — the arrangement Tyler v. Hennepin County held unconstitutional when a government did it. Act 106 of 2024 commissioned a working group on exactly this and did not change the law. Colorado abolished its deed remainder in July 2024 and Minnesota rewrote its scheme in the same year. A Vermont position underwritten on keeping the equity is exposed to one bill.

TOWNS RUN THESE SALES, NOT COUNTIES. Vermont's 246 towns and cities each collect their own delinquent taxes and hold their own sales; the county in a Vermont listing is geography, not the taxing authority. Expect the collector, the notice practice and the sale terms to vary town by town.

SMALL DEBTS NO LONGER REACH SALE. Act 73 of 2025 bars a collector from extending a warrant to begin a tax sale unless the taxpayer owes at least $1,500 in back taxes, and Act 106 requires the town to offer a reasonable written repayment plan first. Act 182 additionally prohibits a sale on residential property while a Vermont Homeowner Assistance Program application is pending, with a separate notice sixty days ahead. Inventory here is filtered by all three before it appears.
The 12% runs on the purchase price, not on the tax debt, so unlike Colorado a Vermont bidder who pays above the debt still earns on the whole amount. The tier reflects that.

WA.assessmentBasis: RCW 84.40.030: "All property must be valued at one hundred percent of its true and fair value in money and assessed on the same basis unless specifically provided otherwise by law." RCW 84.41.030 requires annual revaluation of all taxable real property, with physical inspection at least once every six years.
WA.derivedArvCaveat: This is the most trustworthy derived ARV in the file — full market value, revalued every year — but the parcel is only physically inspected once every six years, so an annual revaluation is a model applied to a property nobody has looked at recently. On a tax-foreclosure parcel, where deterioration is the norm and is exactly what a model of comparable sales will miss, the assessment is likely to describe a building in better condition than the one being sold. Farm, agricultural, timber and open space land also has its own valuation basis outside RCW 84.40.030 and will sit far below market.
WA.statute: RCW 84.64.050 (certificate of delinquency and foreclosure), 84.64.070 (redemption before sale; three-year disability exception), 84.64.080 (sale, minimum bid, surplus, treasurer's deed); RCW 84.40.030 (valuation at 100%), 84.41.030 (annual revaluation)
caveats: A WASHINGTON TAX DEED CAN BE UNWOUND FOR THREE YEARS AND THE RECORD WILL NOT WARN YOU. RCW 84.64.070: "If the real property of any minor, or any person adjudicated to be legally incompetent, be sold for nonpayment of taxes, the same may be redeemed at any time within three years after the date of sale." Nothing in a title search reveals that a former owner was a minor or had been adjudicated incompetent, so this is a latent claim on every Washington parcel for three years. It is the reason quietTitle is marked required in a state whose deed is otherwise clean.

The minimum bid is low, which is the opposite of Ohio. RCW 84.64.080: "The acceptable minimum bid must be the total amount of taxes, interest, and costs." There is no appraisal floor and no market-value floor, so a Washington sale can clear well below value — the discount that Ohio's fair-market-value floor forecloses.

Recorded water-sewer district liens come out of the surplus before the former owner is paid (RCW 84.64.080), which means they are satisfied from the proceeds rather than following the parcel. Surplus above the minimum bid is refunded to the record owner on application, unclaimed after three years going to the county current expense fund — so Washington was already on the right side of Tyler v. Hennepin County.

WI.assessmentBasis: Wis. Stat. § 70.32(1) requires real property to be valued at the full value which could ordinarily be obtained at private sale, and § 70.05(5)(b) requires each taxation district to assess at full value at least once in every 5-year period. The Department of Revenue computes the actual assessed-to-full-value ratio for every district annually under § 70.05(5)(c) and notifies districts that drift more than 10% off over four years.
WI.derivedArvCaveat: Wisconsin's assessment ratio is set per taxation district — town, village or city — and there are roughly 1,850 of them, so it cannot be expressed in countyAssessmentRatios, which is keyed by county FIPS. The 1.0 here is a deliberate floor rather than a measured figure: between revaluations a district's assessments typically lag the market, which makes a derived Wisconsin ARV conservative. The Department of Revenue publishes the real ratio for every district each year, and on a parcel where the number matters it is worth looking up — particularly in a district that has just revalued, where the assessment jumps to full value in a single year.
WI.statute: Wis. Stat. §§ 75.521 (in rem foreclosure, title vesting), 75.35 (sale of tax-deeded lands), 75.69 (advertising, appraised value, sale for any amount after re-advertisement), 75.36 (surplus proceeds), 70.32 and 70.05 (assessment at full value); 2023 Wisconsin Act 207
caveats: A WISCONSIN LISTING CAN BE TAKEN BACK BY ITS FORMER OWNER BEFORE IT SELLS. 2023 Wisconsin Act 207 requires every county to adopt an ordinance letting a former owner, their beneficiaries or heirs repurchase land lost to a tax deed by paying the county's costs, the taxes that would have accrued while the county held it, and the amounts needed to satisfy liens at foreclosure. The ordinance must cover single-family owner-occupied property and may cover everything else. The right is exercised before the county's sale, so it does not cloud a completed purchase — but it means the best inventory is filtered out before auction and a listing can disappear.

THE SECOND PASS HAS NO FLOOR. § 75.69 requires the appraised value to be advertised and bars a sale below it unless the county board or its committee has reviewed and approved the sale. But a county may also "sell for any amount any land previously advertised for sale after advertising the sale of such land by publication of a class 1 notice". A parcel on its second advertisement is a different proposition from one on its first, and nothing in the listing data distinguishes them.

THE COUNTY DOES NOT HAVE TO TAKE THE HIGHEST BID. Under § 75.69 a county may accept less than the highest bid provided the board or its committee "prepares a written statement, available for public inspection, that explains the reasons". Winning on price is not the same as winning.

The county is under a clock, which is unusual and helpful. § 75.69 requires tax-delinquent real estate to be advertised within 180 days of acquisition, reduced from 240 days beginning in 2026. Wisconsin counties cannot sit on inventory the way land banks elsewhere can.

Surplus belongs to the former owner under § 75.36, as amended by Act 207 to net out real estate agent and broker fees and other actual costs of sale, and to offset other delinquent taxes the former owner owes the county. This does not affect the buyer.

WY.assessmentBasis: W.S. 39-13-103: property used for industrial purposes is assessed at 11.5% of fair market value; all other property, real and personal, at 9.5%. Wyoming assesses by use, not by county.
WY.derivedArvCaveat: Two things pull a Wyoming derived ARV in opposite directions. Industrial property is assessed at 11.5% rather than 9.5%, so dividing by 0.095 overstates it by about 1.2x — the dangerous direction. And since tax year 2025 a homeowner claiming the exemption in W.S. 39-11-105(a)(xlvi) has 25% of fair market value exempted, capped at the first $1,000,000, so an owner-occupied assessment reflects roughly three quarters of value and a derived ARV understates it — the safe direction, but by a quarter. Neither is visible in a bare assessed figure; check the assessor's record.
WY.statute: W.S. 39-13-108 (enforcement: tax lien sales, certificates of purchase, redemption and tax deeds); W.S. 39-13-103 (assessment rates); W.S. 39-11-105(a)(xlvi) (homeowner exemption, 2025 Enrolled Act No. 60)
caveats: NO BIDDING. Wyoming allocates liens by random draw rather than auction — the certificate is taxes plus costs and the return does not depend on competition. Our own calendar records Uinta County's procedure as 'Random Selection'. A model that assumes premium or bid-down behaviour does not apply here.

A FURTHER 3% PENALTY IS EARNED IN THE FIRST YEAR, on top of the 15% per annum, and is not in the tier — one number cannot hold both. Year one is therefore better than modelled and years two to four are as modelled.

FOUR YEARS BEFORE A DEED, SIX BEFORE THE RIGHT LAPSES. The holder may apply for a tax deed only after four years from the sale and not more than six. Capital is committed for at least four years, the owner may redeem throughout, and a holder who sleeps past six loses the ability to take title at all.

Wyoming is the longest hold in this file. At 15% simple that is attractive on paper, but auctionToMarketableMonths is 54 and the money is illiquid throughout — compare against what else that capital could do over four and a half years rather than against a one-year lien state.
Assessment is by use, not county: 11.5% industrial, 9.5% everything else. This row uses 9.5%.

The 2025 homeowner exemption (W.S. 39-11-105(a)(xlvi), Enrolled Act No. 60) exempts 25% of fair market value on a single family residence and its improved land, capped at the first $1,000,000, first applying to tax year 2025; from tax year 2026 the claimant must actually reside there at least eight months of the year. Note this is an EXEMPTION, not a rate change — press reporting of an 8.3% owner-occupied rate described a floor amendment that did not survive into the enrolled act.
